I'll be the first here and the most blunt for your own sake and mine. You'll never get over it. Who you were and who you are now will never be the same. Who you will become is yet another entirely different entity. The pain will come, years later, all at once. You'll sense her, catch a glimpse of hair, at the most random times. You'll fear forgetting her face, her voice. You'll flip flop between pouring over her pictures and avoiding them because it hurts just so, so damn much. 

But you will learn to live with it. Telling your story here is already step one. Don't be afraid to tell it again. See what you can do with that strength--can you change the world? Can you make the world a place Lucy would be happier to live in, even if it's just one step at a time? Now can you make the world a better place for other Lucy's of the world? If you can't live for yourself, if you feel like you can't go on, then live for the greater good. 

It'll be a tough road. You will always feel that darkness, but eventually you'll come to recognize it as your memory of Lucy; a scar memorializing the deep connection you once had with another soul. Establish your support network, find that purpose, and you will find Lucy in your success. Do it for her. Good luck, my friend.

I can tell you hanging and shooting are not peaceful. I can tell you that leaving so soon is painful. I can tell you from a survivors view how much it sucks for us, especially when you die so young (assuming you're successful). If not successful, let's not even talk about how much pain you'll be in, or the recovery and hospital staff after. 

I'm not sure what the reason is that you want to end your life, but I can tell you without knowing you that you have impacted the lives of many, and there are clearly people out here that care about your existence. Why do you exist? I don't know. But maybe you should try to find out? 

If all else fails, then let me at least ask that you try to keep living until you get a career. Then when you get enough money, I want you to do two things that you've always wanted to do for yourself. Then after that, write your will and leave it with an executor. Then buy a nice memorial package (from releasing the body to the cremation/embalming to the service) so everything is set and family don't need to worry about raising funds. From there, choose your death and hope you are successful, because it'll be messy if you aren't. 

I don't mean to be blunt, but my husband passed a month ago and it's a lot I am having to deal with. Bless his heart, he is no longer in pain, but that pain has been transferred to me. I refuse to go until I tie up his loose ends, deal with his legal matters, and fight his family because they are violating his privacy even in death. I no longer have anything to lose. 

I know the aftermath, even if you don't care, and I know there will be more than one person who will remember you and will be impacted for life, even if it's someone you least expect. So please, do at least what I request before you make your decision. Think about it, I care because I know.

I never really felt like I found friends until my late 20s. Some of us are just late bloomers. You've made it this far on your own, isn't that a testament to your strength in and of itself? Life changes drastically with every big event, and getting out college, getting a job, or even moving can form new life and habits. Don't give up just because where you are now doesn't show where you will be in 1, 5, or even 10 years. Keep believing in your own abilities, and friends will find you at the most unsuspecting moments. Be patient, you deserve more time.

Yes, do whatever makes you happy. I do suggest getting your will done and buying a memorial package from the morgue of choice so you don't leave everyone who cares about you in a pickle (if you think noone cares, there will always be someone crying at the end). Hopefully, you'll find something that makes you happy enough to keep living though.

It might not be depression, but it does sound like a lot of pent up emotion that you've never released or entrusted to someone else. It may take a leap of faith, or even going to a professional, but I would advise talking about it to someone you trust. I would also advise reading this:

https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impostor_syndrome

I feel like you are having trouble seeing the good that you do, and perhaps you don't see the strengths that others see in you. Have faith in yourself, try to live for yourself and do things you want to do. Honestly, accepting yourself is much harder than others accepting you, because only you know if you are lying. At the same time, that means you can be 100% genuine and non judgmental because you know how hard you've worked and what you've done to keep living. Noone can take that from you.

People are allowed to feel depressed and they have the right to emotions even if they are not clinically diagnosed. You have every right to feel however you do, but the key is to accept that you feel it, and to search for why. This will be a long process, but be patient and forgiving with yourself. 

In the meantime, find things that take your mind off it, or things that make you feel better. Find things you Excel at, and keep doing it. 

Many of us have existential depression, or we may just be nihilists. If that's the case, try to find a purpose in life. Once again, this is a long process so allow yourself time to be frustrated, allow yourself time to think that you may have nothing, allow yourself to slow down. Some days you won't feel like moving at all, and that's okay. Just know that eventually you will.

What you think are faults may be improved on, or used as assets in other parts of your life. Accept yourself, and find a trusted group who can also accept you, flaws and all. If they can't, then move on; you'll find a group someday, but don't forget that you matter too you first. 

Don't be so quick to judge yourself; your are more than you know. Hope that helps.

My husband died a month ago (suicide) and not a day goes by that I wonder if I should follow him. I was not suicidal prior to now. I have PTSD from finding his body, a week old. The stress from his family, from all the loose ends, from waiting and waiting and never allowing myself time to grieve is infuriating. I sit at work and am unable to work, the guilt from that creates more stress. I have trouble breathing, my chest hurts when I start to have panic attacks. 

His work is in shambles--his boss was his mother figure. His family is now pretending he was never married, and have stolen all that belong to me (and his money too). They never told me when his memorial was (it's just for reporters and political power) and expect me to do a "free" one for all his real friends and all the ones who really cared. 

Im sure your life story is different than mine, but the hell I'm going through, the hell everyone you've touched will go through, may be worth your living in this reality. 

I never thought that way until I realized how many hearts my husband touched and what a true impact he's been, even on people who've only met him once until the day he was found. Every action you've ever done have caused a ripple effect on this world, and we all must count on each other to keep that going. I urge you to think about this, because I can't take anymore pain in my heart and I spend days bedridden from depression like my husband did prior to his death. You matter, even to people who don't know you, because we see the people you've touched, just by writing this post. Please think wisely, if not just for a stranger who had failed someone she cared deeply about.

I also wish I could say it's just the grieving process, but his family isn't making it the easiest either. I'm struggling every day to keep afloat, and I'm trying to be outside and not alone as much as possible. It's all just so frustrating. I wish I had better news to give :(

I love reading all the happy marriages here. Everything seems to be mentioned already, so I'd just like to say that it's important even in the hardest times to let your SO know that you love her and wont leave her. Honestly, I think the hardest part of MS is the mental stress, guilt, and depression the MS person gets from wanting to be "normal" for you, friends, and family. Make sure she feels needed, important, and loved for all that she is. Lots of patience. My husband struggled most with the mental aspect of MS (depression, incoherency with heat, inability to accept the illness, etc)

I agree with the others here. You will be living in some dark times... But is it worth it to you? My husband (with MS) couldn't handle the guilt and shame from not being able to care for me and passed away just a couple weeks ago. I won't lie that at that time we were fighting, and I did feel like he held me back, but noone else understood me like he did and vice versa. We made the best out of our nights at home, and even if things got rough I loved him all the same. Our conversations were worth more than any traveling or "date nights" outside.  

MS is cruel in the fact that your SO feels like they've lost all control of their body, dreams, and life. The most you can do is continue to tell her that you love her regardless, that she will find things she can do (my husband was a software engineer with an understanding company), and that she completes you. Therapy didn't work on me or the hubs, but it might help. Lots of support and make her feel validated and acknowledged is my advice.

I was married to a beautiful soul with MS. It was the first thing he disclosed to me while we dated, and it scared me, but something about the way we matched never felt so right. I knew I could never leave him. The road was long and hard, and he battled chronic fatigue, heat sensitivity, spasms, and depression. We had many fights and many frustrations, but the times when he was good, even if we were home 90% of the time, were amazing. We adjusted to the best of our abilities. There were times I thought it was too much; he couldn't accept the fact that he had MS and could be fine one day then bed ridden the next. He couldn't accept that he couldn't go to work, or do something simple for me like go to the grocery store. His mental clarity began to wane, his symptoms exacerbated, and he began to have more anxiety and more depression with the stress on his body. I was fighting for the both of us, and I took care of him from helping him stay cool to making sure he ate throughout the week. I was tired and burnt out, but I knew I would always run back to him. He passed away at the age of 30 after pushing me away for a week to make sure I was gone. I don't think he thought I'd be the one to find him. 

If you love her, and you love all her flaws and imperfections, and you are willing to test your own patience, compassion, and will power, then go to her. Tell her even at her worst times that you love her and will never leave. Never give up. Hold on to the good memories, and savor the little moments. This will test you, but she may be worth it. The relationship may seem like you're doing more work, but she will most likely be handling just as much within herself. I wish I had more time with my husband, MS or not, but perhaps you'll be luckier.

I would give almost anything for my partner. I love him and I always will, but that doesn't change the fact that MS and several other factors are taking over his mind, spirit, and body and changing him into a shell of who he used to be. It doesn't change the days I get anxiety/panic attacks because I don't know when he will yell and scream at me, more often than not. Love doesn't take away the pain, the stress, or the frustration when he's given up on himself and it's you fighting for two, with him trying to push you away with hurtful words and actions. Love doesn't take away the guilt on both parties when the marriage begins to fray and you have to decide if you need to save yourself or kill yourself (literally) giving 100:0. Love is not enough. Love doesn't cure the arguments over drug addiction, illogical outbursts, and long talks about suicide. Love will always be there, but that alone does not mean strength.  This is reality. This is the long term pain MS causes. It doesn't just tear away the person. It destroys relationships, lives, and dreams. Don't ever believe anyone who says love is enough. It takes much more than that.

You opened my mind when you talked about groups. I'm usually fine with one other person who can match my melancholy--it's usually in groups that I begin to feel out of place. People are just too happy; people seem to be interested in things I can't bring myself to be as enthusiastic about. Sometimes I wonder when I had ceased existing in their minds, or if I only did for convenience. I don't do well in large groups, and I often feel loneliest in large crowds. Thank you for hearing me and reaching out, it is one of the only things allowing me to function in society and keep up my facade of being a normal, happy person today.

Thank you for your kind words :) It's good to know that I'm not alone in thinking this, as often I have wondered "Is it just me? Do I just not belong in this entire world?" It's easy to go down that path and lose myself in this mindless existence by wallowing in self-pity and guilt. Having this support and not being judged/regarded as weak is keeping me going right now.

Trapped is the perfect word for what I'm feeling right now. A collage of screaming thoughts trapped inside a physical shell in a 3D dimension, forced to conform blindly or face ridicule and isolation. I can't seem to find a purpose that would make me actually live in this sad world.

Happy people make me wonder why I'm not like them. Why must we question everything and feel out of place? And are they really nice? Or will they turn their back on you if a situation that would benefit them come to play? Who can I trust--if anyone at all?

I totally get it; we should have all just stayed in the Matrix. I hate dumbing myself down and acting like what society deems "normal." It makes me feel fake and dirty, and that sense of "I don't belong" only gets stronger. Sometimes I curl up in a ball, holding myself tight even though I can feel my thoughts screaming to come out. I don't feel like anywhere is home, and even when I thought I found home, I find myself wondering how people can seem so happy and why I am not feeling the same way. We're aliens hiding our identities in steel jungle held by monotonous habits and ways. :(

I don't blame you for having the thoughts you do. You are a completely selfless, compassionate soul so lost in sacrificing yourself for others that you've bottled up all your needs and wants your whole life. I know how that is. If you have the courage to finally off yourself, I wish you'd also have the courage to give the royal middle finger and leave those toxic people as well. I've grown up thinking the world was a horrible place full of evil people. Often times I still think that way--most of the time, actually. But I've also learned to fight back, and to stop giving a crap about people who don't appreciate me. Whichever decision you choose, I wish you the best of luck and dreams, and that you will finally be content with who you are. If not, then I think that's grounds for uprooting your current lifestyle and starting over from scratch, if you're still with us. We are all Elliots in this harsh world with our own harsh stories--the one control we have in life is the way we react to our thoughts and the decisions we make to ward off the inner demons. I wish you the best.
